summary:
The penal code in force since 15 November 2022 does not explicitly criminalise same-sex intimacy or gender diversity. Same-sex sexual activity is lawful and the age of consent is 18 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. The code is a revision of a historic-era Spanish criminal code dating to the Francoist period. Article 364(2) bars employment discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, the first provision explicitly protecting lesbian, gay and bisexual people, and Law 1/2016 on the Protection of Personal Data (Articles 10 and 41) protects personal data on 'sexual life' where it entails discrimination.

Enforcement does not follow the statute. Authorities continue to apply the obsolete 1954 Law on Vagrants and Criminals, which classifies homosexuality as an illness and normalises conversion practices. A 2020 draft law, 'Regulating Prostitution and the Rights of Homosexuals', would move the conduct squarely into the criminal code if enacted; its status is unresolved. Three further instruments institutionalise discrimination against LGBT people: the Military Justice Code, a ministerial order on 'immoral' activities, and a provincial regulation. ILGA reports that state intimidation of sexually diverse individuals persists: no law explicitly criminalises homosexuality, yet LGBTQ+ people are detained and punished through public shaming.

Police and military intervene in the spaces of assembly, expression and residence of lesbian women. In Bata, police detain known lesbians collectively, on the premise that 'lesbians are members of a sect', and apply collective punishment when one lesbian is sought. Transgender women have reported harassment and sexual violence while in police custody, and security forces have subjected LGBTQ+ people to sexual violence and discrimination in the military, in jails and in prison.

Documented incidents give the pattern its shape. In 2014 four men were detained over a video found on a phone and made to explain their actions on national television. A lesbian couple in Añisok were tied up at the police station, paraded through town with banners calling them witchcraft-practicing lesbians, photographed and shamed. In August 2023 police illegally detained Trifonia Melibea Obono, founder of Somos Parte del Mundo, after her group submitted a report on torture and ill-treatment of LGBTQI+ people to the EU headquarters in Madrid; arrests and restrictions rose significantly afterward.

Rape is sometimes used as a form of conversion therapy, and queer women are forcibly impregnated in an attempt to make them heterosexual. LGBTQ+ women and transgender men are described as vulnerable to sexual violence in the military and from family. Laws against rape are not effectively enforced: the crime is rarely reported, and police and judicial officials may decline to act where the perpetrator has political connections or is in the police or military.

The 2021 US State Department report, which predates the current penal code, recorded that same-sex conduct was not specifically criminalised but that LGBT persons faced societal stigma, with no anti-discrimination protections, within a general context of repression. Same-sex couples have no legal recognition and are not eligible for the same legal protections available to opposite-sex couples. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local birth-sex status has no access to partnership recognition or the protections attached to it.
tangentialFactors:
A stakeholder submission to the country's fourth UN human rights review, filed by Small Media, EG Justice, IPI and Digital Rights in Equatorial Guinea, documents restrictions on freedom of expression, digital rights and journalist safety. The same repressive environment constrains LGBT advocacy and organising, and it shapes how visible any visitor or resident can afford to be.

An analysis in Hispanic Studies Review (October 2025) of Trifonia Melibea Obono's 2019 novel 'Yo no quería ser madre' finds compulsory heterosexuality and queer invisibility in the social climate. The finding describes the conditions under which queer and trans people live rather than any legal rule.
localsOnly:
LGBTQ+ people face discrimination in education and employment. Teachers have reportedly discriminated against and excluded LGBTQ+ girls, and school officials have reportedly denied transgender students access to some facilities. Academics and government employees can be ousted if perceived as not heterosexual. LGBTQ+ children are often forced out of their homes, which frequently causes them to drop out of school.

Transgender children are especially vulnerable to commercial sexual exploitation according to a local NGO, and minors generally are sexually exploited for commercial sex.

Conversion practices operate through the 1954 Law on Vagrants and Criminals, which treats homosexuality as an illness. Rape is used in some cases as a form of conversion therapy, and queer women are forcibly impregnated in an attempt to make them heterosexual.
outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the 2020 draft law 'Regulating Prostitution and the Rights of Homosexuals' is unresolved in the sources; whether it has been enacted, withdrawn or left dormant is not established.

No sourced information was identified on legal gender recognition, document or marker change, hormone access, medication or trans-specific health services.

No sourced information was identified on entry and visa rules, or on airport and security screening practices that would affect trans travellers differentially.

No sourced data was identified on trans-specific violence with a denominator that would allow comparison against the general homicide rate.
